I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

prediction.raw: **1 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why, factually and ethically:** ### ️ **You were absolutely justified in refusing** - **"Help" ≠ " doing her job for her while she watches."** - If she genuinely needed assistance (e.g., the box was too heavy *for both of you*), she should have ** actively participated** in the lift (e.g., bracing, stabilizing, or helping hoist). - Instead, she asked you to ** solo-lift a 4-foot-high box while she stood idle**. That’s not teamwork—it’s ** shifting her responsibilities onto you**. - * Workplace safety protocols often require *two people* for heavy lifting to prevent injury (e.g., proper form, balanced weight distribution). By not helping, *she* was actually making the task * more dangerous* for you. - **"We’re both paid for the same job" is correct.** - If the role requires lifting heavy boxes (as stated in your description), ** she should be capable of doing it herself**. - Employers don’t assign "designated heavy lifters" for routine tasks like this. If she can’t perform core duties, ** she should address it with HR**— not expect others to cover for her. - **Your response to the senior coworker was professional:** - "I’m not the designated heavy lifter... let’s discuss this with HR" is ** exactly how you should handle it**. - HR would almost certainly agree: ** expecting one person to do all the physical labor while another observes is not " teamwork"— it’s unfair and unsafe.** ### ❌ **Why the senior coworker and FCW are wrong** - **"Next time someone asks for help, you need to help them" is a misapplication of " teamwork."** - True teamwork means ** shared effort**. If she genuinely couldn’t lift it (e.g., due to a disability or injury), she should have * explained* and * asked for *collaborative* help* (e.g., "Can you help me get this into the bin? I need support on my side"). - But she didn’t. She asked you to ** solo-lift while she stood there**. That’s not " asking for help"— it’s ** asking you to do her job for her**. - * The senior coworker’s " team" comment is a ** toxic misinterpretation of workplace dynamics**. If he genuinely believes this, he’s setting a harmful precedent (e.g., " women can’t do physical work, so men must always do it for them"). - **FCW’s behavior was unprofessional:** - Storming off and " finding someone else" is ** childish and manipulative**. - If she’s physically capable (as described), ** she should be able to lift a 4-foot-high box herself**. If she genuinely can’t, ** she needs to disclose it to HR**— not guilt-trip coworkers into doing her work. ### 💡 **Key takeaway:** - **You were not the asshole.** You set a boundaries for ** fair, safe, and professional collaboration**. - **The real issue is the FCW’s expectation that you should do her job for her**— and the senior coworker’s failure to correct her. - **Next steps:** - If this happens again, ** document it** (e.g., " on [date], FCW asked me to solo-lift a box while she stood idle; I refused because it’s not safe or fair"). - ** escalate to HR** if the senior coworker or FCW persist. HR * should* support you— this is a clear case of ** unreasonably shifting work onto a coworker**. **Final verdict: 1 (Not the asshole)**. You handled this appropriately. The problem lies with her and the senior coworker’s mis understanding of " teamwork." 💪
